title: I Am Not Stanley Kubrick
excerpt: On the gap between taste and authorship, Kubrick's unglamorous early years, and a fantasy about a pill that fixes none of it.
body:
Bradley Cooper in his film Limitless takes an ultra-nootropic called NZT, which makes him a genius overnight and resolves his mired creative block. I too am in a mired creative block, not because I'm not producing anything (I am) but because my work is not me. Ira Glass articulated this problem in one of the most repeated musings on the creative process: that creative people, early on, suck – and they know it.

I cannot make 2001: A Space Odyssey (at least currently). Kubrick couldn't have either, at seventeen, when he was photographing shoeshine boys and dentists' offices. I mean, the man had to make Fear and Desire before he made The Shining. I guess he also played a lot of chess? Personally, I've shot only minute-long reels that rely on ironic conventions and lighting gimmicks, and I also suck at chess.

Kubrick had a truly distinct "eye" for things, which shows in how unusually he composed dreadful subjects with complete symmetry. My eyes, on the other hand, are more developed than my "eye." I can tell you with precision exactly what Kubrick does and why, but I'd laser you if you had me explain my shot angles.

Still, if I made a feature film, it would follow a voyager who tries on every costume of life: quant analysis at hedge funds, art curator at the Getty, years of meditation in Kathmandu, and a whole decade of sleeping between doses of crack cocaine. The vastness of culture would be a deep curiosity waiting for a colour grade.

Between eighty years of life and psychological determinism, a mind can only hold so much. Movies, music, and books are ways of seeing precisely because you cannot crawl into my brain. But if I could write like Chekhov, cut film like Kubrick, and compose like Bach, you'd think maybe you did.

So yes, if I were offered NZT, I would take it. With my newfound scientific prowess – which would no doubt land me a lab at MIT named after myself – I would engineer a solution to clean the nootropic of side effects and start a private production chain. I would then learn to encode my rugged sadness in the bends of a guitar, write a modern Ovid's Metamorphoses better than the original, and make fourteen feature films.

But if I want to make my own 2001 without altering my synapses with a fictitious nootropic, I have to make work, and lots of it. I have done that today, sort of: articulated my grand ambitions onto a Google Doc in Times New Roman, of all fonts.

Why have I done this at 4 AM? Maybe I'm micro-micro-dosing NZT. Or maybe writing is what you do when you have no motion on Hinge and a plaguing realisation that Ira Glass is right.

Alas, my mother doesn't understand my urge to "make great art." When I told her the story of Kafka's Metamorphosis, she scoffed and asked me not to read "such books." Then she said she'd love me even if I turned into a giant insect. Ah, Mother. What can I say!

title: Shut Up
body:
You can whisper loudly. It's true. Vocal cords may be out of the equation but I can hear you. The air is noisy enough.

A library is where you focus. Anything can be done with focus. You can have a conversation, watch a movie, have sex with focus. You probably should. But not in a library. This is not your room.

We all expect focus in a library. Your focus should not compromise my focus. That's why most people use libraries to do their own work.

There are exceptions to this norm.

But exceptions aren't howling in a library. Nobody is.

Shouldn't we have a loudness ceiling instead of enforcing pin-drop silence like maniacs. Sometimes you need to ask the librarian where a book is. Sometimes you meet your long-lost high-school sweetheart and they're beautiful and you need to say something — anything.

Alas, libraries have digital book-search systems and librarians have ID cards — in which case, anyone on a glance will understand you need something — and most loud whisperers are not talking to Ananya from School.

The problem is this. The term "loud whisper" is a paradox. If I can hear your whisper from another table, it's not really a whisper — at least functionally. 30-40db, roughly how loud this category of sounds is, is definitely above my noise ceiling.

If that's not the case for you, I'm sorry. I thought we were sharing the library.
